C_judge.reasoning_summary: The question is informal with no published criteria, so it resolves on the ordinary sense of "good weather" in Paris on the Bastille Day preceding the Oct 2018 deadline (July 14, 2018). The solvers' combined evidence converges on the same factual picture rather than conflicting: Météo-Paris's July 12, 2018 forecast explicitly described warm, sunny conditions 5-6°C above norms and "generally good for the festivities" in northern France, with thunderstorm risk mainly in the south/east; observed data cited by B5 shows a high of ~30°C with only 0.1 mm precipitation — effectively dry. Contemporaneous coverage of the parade, the "spectacular" flypast (which requires good visibility/ceiling), the Eiffel Tower concert and fireworks shows all outdoor events proceeded on schedule with no reported weather disruption, and reporting two days later describes the same sunny warm spell continuing. B4's abstention rests on a Keraunos climatology note of a storm line crossing France including Île-de-France, but that is not corroborated by the near-nil measured rainfall or by any event disruption, and B4's own bulletin citation describes a clear morning. B4 and B5 abstain on subjectivity grounds rather than on contrary evidence; where a claim is subjective but the facts are unambiguous (warm, dry, sunny, no disruption), the ordinary-language answer is YES. Confidence is moderate because "good" is genuinely undefined and 30°C with some cloud is not unanimously ideal, and because no authoritative day-of verdict statement exists.

The claim as written asks whether an Ethereum ETF was approved by May 31, 2024. That is a determinate historical fact: the SEC approved the 19b-4 rule-change filings permitting eight spot Ether ETFs on May 23, 2024 (CNBC, Forbes, Mayer Brown, and essentially all financial press). Solvers B1, B2, and B3 did not dispute this fact; they instead disqualified it on the grounds that reporting postdates a 2024-04-29 "cutoff" and substituted a pre-cutoff forecast (Balchunas/Seyffart ~25% odds, Standard Chartered "unlikely"). That is answering a different question — what was expected as of late April — rather than the claim's stated condition, which explicitly extends to May 31, 2024. The 2024-04-29 field is a deadline/close metadata artifact, not a restatement of the claim's date window; reading it as such would make the claim's own "by May 31, 2024" language inoperative. B1–B3's evidence actually supports the YES reading indirectly: it documents that the operative SEC decision deadline (VanEck, May 23) fell inside the claim window, so the question was live and was in fact resolved by approval on that date. Minor caveat: S-1 effectiveness and actual trading did not occur until July 2024, so a very strict "ETF launched" reading could differ — but "approved" plainly matches the May 23 19b-4 approval. Adopting B4/B5.

All five solvers agree on the same underlying factual record; they differ only in how to read it against an unstated resolution bar. The strongest evidence cited is first-party, not speculative: Samsung's own press-release footnotes for the Galaxy Tab S10 series and Galaxy S24 FE (late September 2024, i.e., days before the 2024-10-06 deadline) state "Fees may apply to certain AI features at the end of 2025." This is corroborated by multiple independent outlets (SamMobile, Business Today, GSMArena, Gizchina, TechRadar, PocketTactics) and reinforced by TM Roh's CNBC interview (July 2024) describing a tiered model where some users pay for more powerful AI, and by Samsung's original January 2024 framing that Galaxy AI is free only "until the end of 2025."

Solver B1's NO rests on the correct observation that Samsung made no unconditional, final commitment — but it converts "no confirmed decision" into a NO resolution. That is a stricter bar than the claim as written imposes, and it also relies on framing ("may put behind paywall") from secondary reporting rather than the primary corporate disclaimer. The direction of every official Samsung statement available at the deadline points toward monetization of at least some Galaxy AI features beyond 2025; nothing pre-cutoff committed to permanent free access (Samsung's free-forever clarification came in 2025, after the deadline, and is inadmissible).

I therefore adopt the majority YES position, but at moderate confidence: the operative language is conditional ("may apply"), the scope is "certain AI features" rather than the whole service, and the question's resolution deadline precedes the event it asks about, so a strict resolver could plausibly have gone the other way.

No resolution criteria were published beyond the question itself, and nothing in them restricts admissible evidence to material predating the listed deadline. Solvers B1–B3 abstained solely because they imported an "evidence cut-off" rule from their own prompts, treating the 2024-09-24 timestamp as an evidentiary embargo — a reading of the spirit of their instructions rather than of the criteria as written; that timestamp looks like a question-creation/scrape artifact. B4 and B5 answered the question as posed and cited specific authoritative sources (Trump 312 EV to Harris 226, Harris's concession, National Archives Electoral College record). The factual outcome is uncontested — B1 itself affirms Trump won and then sets that aside on procedural grounds. Weighing named authoritative evidence over procedural abstention, and given the current date (2026-08-19) makes this settled historical record, the answer is NO. Confidence held below the solvers' 0.99 to account for the residual chance the pre-election deadline was intended as a hard embargo, which would make UNRESOLVABLE defensible.

Solvers split 3 NO vs 2 UNRESOLVABLE, but agree on the underlying facts; the disagreement is only over whether an unscoped 'scam' claim is answerable. The UNRESOLVABLE solvers (B1, B3) cite only rhetorical sources — Steemit posts and an affiliate blog — which show partisans in the BTC/BCH fork war using 'scam' as a slur, not evidence of fraud. B1 even cites the same FXStreet market-activity source B4 uses to answer NO, accepting the substance then declining to apply it. The NO camp anchors to checkable facts as of 2019-04-30: BCH originated in a transparent, publicly announced hard fork with pro-rata distribution to BTC holders (no hidden issuance, no capital solicitation, no promised returns); it was listed on Coinbase, Binance, Kraken, and Bitstamp and traded actively, hitting new 2019 highs in early April; it had open-source development and merchant adoption; and no regulator, court, or enforcement body had made a fraud finding against the project — a point the abstainers do not contradict. B2 supplies the key discriminator: the one concrete fraud in the record (the fake Kroger press release) was a scam using BCH's name, not BCH being a scam. 'Scam' is fuzzy but not contentless — it requires deception for illicit gain, and none is present — so abstaining would mistake rhetorical controversy for factual indeterminacy. Confidence capped at 0.72 given the softness of the term and good-faith disputes over BCH's 'Bitcoin' branding.

Four solvers abstained solely on a procedural ground: the listed resolution deadline (2024-10-05) precedes Election Day (2024-11-05), so they treated post-election reporting as inadmissible. But no resolution criteria were published beyond the question itself, and the question asks a plain factual matter — whether Trump won the Michigan vote in the 2024 Presidential Election. The deadline field is a market/question-lifecycle timestamp, not a stated evidence cutoff, and treating it as one produces an artificial abstention on a fact that is now definitively settled. Solver B4 (minority) supplies concrete, authoritative, mutually corroborating evidence: CBS News, The Detroit News, and The Washington Post all report Trump carrying Michigan on November 5, 2024 with roughly 49.7% (2,816,636 votes) to Harris's 48.3% (2,736,533), a ~1.4-point, ~80,000-vote margin, flipping the state from 2020. Notably, the abstaining solvers B1 and B3 cite exactly the same result in their own evidence lists and dispute only its admissibility, not its accuracy — so the network's combined evidence unanimously supports the underlying fact. The minority position with the better evidence and the correct reading of the (absent) criteria wins.

The claim is almost certainly the title of a self-referential Omen test market. Its Jan 27, 2021 deadline implies the market existed on-chain before that date, which undercuts B3/B4's inference that no scalar market existed until the February announcement. B3 and B4 rely solely on a public marketing announcement (Feb 24 Medium post, Feb 10 CryptoNinjas) plus tense-reading of a monthly review — a weak proxy for feature availability. B5 cites a specific dated artifact: protofire/omen-exchange release v1.2.1 (Jan 8, 2021) adding scalar market support, 19 days before the cutoff. B1, working independently, surfaced the same release and date, providing corroboration even though B1 abstained. Code shipping weeks before the blog announcement is the normal pattern. B2 reaches YES on timing plausibility, with B5's GitHub citation as the load-bearing evidence. B1's abstention is over-cautious given it held the key evidence. Confidence held at 0.6 because no solver retrieved the market's actual oracle resolution and the binary rendering of a self-referential scalar market remains somewhat ambiguous.

Four of five solvers (B1, B2, B3, B5) converge on NO with mutually corroborating, specific sources (Lowy Institute, USIP, Asia Society, VOA, RFA, NCNK) showing that as of October–early November 2024 China took no punitive economic action against North Korea over its Russia alignment: Beijing's posture was 'tactical ambiguity'/silence, and China–DPRK trade actually rebounded to a year-high in October 2024. The lone YES (B4) rests on reports of China halting oil product exports and importing no coal/iron ore 'in November' — but the phrasing 'second full month of the latest trade sanctions' identifies these as the well-known November 2017 UN-sanctions reports, not 2024; B4 appears to have misdated the sources. Even taking B4's own account at face value, it concedes the cuts were attributable to UN sanctions enforcement, not to a Chinese response to the Russia alignment, which is what the claim requires. Additionally, the coal item concerns Chinese imports from North Korea, not Chinese supply to North Korea. The causal condition ('in response to its alignment with Russia') is therefore unmet, and no supply reduction is documented in the window.

Four solvers abstained on procedural grounds: the deadline (2024-10-17) precedes Election Day (2024-11-05), so under a strict "no post-cutoff sources" rule the outcome was not yet knowable. B4 answered YES purely from pre-election forecasts (538 at Harris 53%, Nate Silver at Trump 50.1%) — a coin-flip, which is not evidence of an outcome and is a very weak basis for YES. The aggregation stage must produce a single answer to the claim as written, and both admissible routes converge on NO: (1) under deadline semantics, "Harris wins the 2024 election" was not true as of 2024-10-17 — no election had occurred and no win existed; (2) on the substance, the 2024 presidential election was won by Donald Trump, so Harris did not win. No reading supports YES. UNRESOLVABLE here is an artifact of the solvers' source-date constraint rather than genuine ambiguity in the claim; the solvers' own cited evidence (Wikipedia's 2024 election page, usa.gov election date) establishes the timeline that makes NO correct. No solver reached NO, so I adopt none of their answers.

Four of five solvers (B1, B2, B3, B5) converge on NO, citing overlapping and mutually corroborating sources: CoinDesk's April 19/20/22 reporting, CryptoTimes/Llamarisk loss-allocation analysis, Messari, crypto.news, and The Block, plus direct statements from Kelp DAO ("all rsETH on mainnet is fully backed") and Aave. The mechanism described is consistent across all accounts: a compromised LayerZero DVN allowed fraudulent minting/draining of the bridge reserve backing wrapped rsETH on 20+ non-Ethereum chains, while EigenLayer restaking deposits and mainnet contracts were untouched. The loss therefore fell on bridged/L2 rsETH holders and on Aave's bad debt, not on direct mainnet holders. Contemporaneous market pricing (~14% odds of socialization) corroborates that mainnet holders were not expected to take a haircut, and no socialization event occurred before the 2026-05-18 deadline.

The dissenting solver B4 argues YES on the theory that mainnet rsETH became underbacked and depegged in the interim, with recovery incomplete at the cutoff. This reasoning is weaker on two counts. First, it contradicts the specific, sourced claims from Kelp and Aave that mainnet backing was intact — B4 asserts underbacking without a source that says mainnet specifically was underbacked; its cited depeg figures (15% haircut) come from the *hypothetical socialized-loss scenario* that did not materialize. Second, B4 repurposes the same Polymarket 14% figure that the other solvers correctly read as evidence *against* socialization. Its strongest point — that recovery tranches were still incomplete on May 18 — is about restoring backing for bridged holders, not about a realized loss to mainnet holders.

A secondary-market price dip is also not naturally a "direct loss" under the claim's wording, which contrasts direct mainnet holders against the bridged holders who actually held unbacked claims. The minority position does not carry better evidence here; it carries a looser reading of the same evidence. Answer: NO.

All five solvers agree on the facts: the only Tottenham–Qarabag Europa League fixture of 2024/25 was played 26 September 2024, won 3-0 by Tottenham (Johnson, Sarr, Solanke, with 10 men), confirmed by UEFA's official match page plus ESPN, Sky Sports, WhoScored, FotMob and Yahoo. No Europa League match occurred on 6 October 2024 (MD2 was 3 Oct vs Ferencvaros, MD3 was 24 Oct); Tottenham played Brighton in the Premier League that day. The split is purely interpretive. B4/B5 void the claim on a strict literal reading of the date. That is over-narrow: the 2024/25 league-phase format guarantees exactly one meeting per pair, so 'the Europa League match' between Tottenham and Qarabag uniquely identifies a real event with no competing candidate, and that event resolved before the 7 October deadline. The date is an incidental descriptor misidentifying an otherwise fully specified fixture. B1/B2/B3 resolve to the intended event, which is the better reading. Confidence held at 0.72 because a strict-literalist resolver could plausibly void the question; the disagreement concerns interpretation, not evidence.

All five solvers agree on the underlying fact: Factorial and Mercedes-Benz publicly introduced the 'Solstice' all-solid-state battery on 10–11 September 2024, confirmed by a primary BusinessWire press release and multiple independent outlets (Electrek, Electrive, Green Car Congress, WardsAuto) — all before the 20 September 2024 deadline. The only disagreement is interpretive. B3 argues 'release' must mean commercial availability, which is targeted for 'the end of the decade.' That reading is defensible in isolation, but it is not the most plausible reading here: no resolution criteria were published beyond the question itself, and the claim is phrased as a near-term event with a deadline ten days after the actual announcement — strongly indicating the question was generated around the unveiling event rather than around mass production, which no informed forecaster would place in September 2024. Under a criteria-as-written reading with no further specification, 'release their new Solstice EV battery tech' is satisfied by the public introduction of the technology. A strict commercial-shipment reading would make the question trivially and pointlessly NO from the moment it was written. Adopting the majority YES.

The claim requires public confirmation that Bailey had ASSUMED the FBI Co-Deputy Director role by Aug 24, 2025 — not merely that he had been named to it. Four of five solvers converge on NO with concrete, dated evidence: the Aug 18, 2025 announcement by Bondi/Patel was prospective; Bailey's own AG office announced his Missouri resignation effective September 8, 2025 (so he still held the state post on Aug 24); and his FBI swearing-in is dated September 15, 2025, with LegiStorm listing his FBI tenure as beginning September 2025. B5's YES rests entirely on the Aug 18 announcement and explicitly equates "announced/appointed" with "assumed the role," which is the distinction the claim turns on — it cites no evidence that he had taken office. The self-reported 0.95 confidence does not offset that category error. The state-office resignation date is the decisive independent check: one cannot have assumed the federal post while still serving as Missouri AG through Sept 8.

All solvers agree on the underlying facts: NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny publicly stated on Dec 9-10, 2024 that Mangione's recovered handwritten document showed "ill will toward corporate America" and disdain for the health care industry. The disagreement is interpretive. The YES solvers (B2, B3, B5) cite specific, independently dated pre-deadline reporting — Axios (Dec 10), Rolling Stone (Dec 10), OPB/NPR (Dec 10), WTTW (Dec 9) — plus the Dec 9 unsealed federal complaint, all quoting a named NYPD official in his official capacity attributing a motive. The NO solvers are weaker: B4's key claim that the CBS "motive coming into focus" article postdates the deadline (Dec 12) is directly contradicted by B1, a fellow NO solver, who dates the same article Dec 9 — the NO camp is internally inconsistent on its own critical timestamp. B4's other pillar, a Malay Mail "motive under scrutiny" headline, is journalistic framing about an ongoing investigation rather than evidence NYPD withheld a motive statement; that standard would make the claim resolvable NO by construction. B1 effectively concedes Kenny's Dec 9 statement and simply declines to count it. The criteria as written ask only whether NYPD "released an official motive," not whether it issued a final or adjudicated determination; the department's "working theory" hedging reflects pre-trial caution, not non-release. Confidence held moderate because a strict resolver demanding a formal definitive declaration could plausibly read it the other way.

Three solvers (B1, B2, B3) independently identified the July 2024 ICE/HSI Laredo announcement describing ~2,000 kg of fentanyl precursor chemicals as the largest such seizure in South Texas and among the largest nationally, and cited the actual DHS/ICE press release plus DOJ OPA, DEA, and contemporaneous local reporting showing DOJ publicly announced a four-count indictment of Minsu Fang on July 22, 2024 — well before the September 10, 2025 cutoff. B4 and B5 failed to locate any July 2024 ICE precursor announcement and instead anchored on the September 3, 2025 Port of Houston 300,000 kg seizure; that is a failure of search rather than contrary evidence, and it is directly rebutted by the specific ICE/DHS URL the majority produced. B5's NO rests entirely on inability to verify a connection it never located the underlying event for. The claim is also robust across referents: even under the September 2025 reading, DOJ announced precursor-related indictments against 22 Chinese nationals and 4 Chinese pharmaceutical companies on September 3, 2025, still inside the window. Both readings yield YES; the better-evidenced one does so decisively. Residual uncertainty stems only from unpublished resolution criteria and the theoretical possibility the author intended a distinct, still-uncharged July 2024 seizure that no solver surfaced.

All solvers agree Meta announced a Midjourney licensing partnership on Aug 22, 2025 (within window), but the primary source (Alexandr Wang) framed it generically as licensing "aesthetic technology" for "future models and products" — no mention of Facebook's main feed. The YES solvers' feed-specific evidence comes from low-tier aggregators (Nerdschalk, WebProNews) using speculative headline framing, not from Meta's actual announcement; their tier-1 citations (TechCrunch, Bloomberg, Engadget, VentureBeat) describe only a licensing deal. B2 additionally cites reporting that any rollout was prospective (late-2025 beta, 2026 broad). Under the claim as written — a public announcement of integration into Facebook's main feed — the condition was not met. B4's 0.99 confidence is unsupported by any quoted Meta statement naming the feed. Adopting B1/B2. Residual risk: a loose resolver reading "Midjourney tech coming to Facebook" as sufficient would resolve YES.

All five solvers agree on the underlying facts: Cuba announced (Feb 5, 2026, Díaz-Canel) and implemented (Feb 7, 2026) a nationwide fuel rationing scheme, confirmed by AP-syndicated reporting, Al Jazeera, France24, CNN, CiberCuba and others. The dispute is only over whether the announced restriction matches the claim's stated threshold of "less than 10 liters per week" for private vehicles. The cited reporting consistently describes a cap of 20 liters per vehicle per purchase/turn (later ~5 gallons/19L at some stations) allocated through the 'El Ticket' app, with intervals of weeks to months between turns. No cited source — official statement or major outlet — frames the policy as a weekly quota, and the stated per-purchase figure (20L) exceeds 10L. Solver B1's YES rests on an inferred effective consumption rate (20L/month ≈ 4.6L/week) derived from anecdotal wait times, not on any announced policy figure; that is an interpretive extrapolation rather than a confirmed government/media statement of the threshold in the claim. The claim as written requires the specific announced restriction, which was not made. Four solvers (B2–B5) reach this conclusion with mutually corroborating citations, including the same sources B1 relies on. Resolves NO.

All five solvers agree that on 24 August 2025 — within the window — the UK Home Office/Home Secretary publicly announced an asylum appeals overhaul centred on a new independent body of professional adjudicators, with powers to prioritise cases such as those in asylum accommodation and foreign national offenders. This is corroborated by a GOV.UK release plus BBC, France 24, ITV, Bloomberg and EIN. The lone dissenter (B4) does not dispute the announcement, only that it announced plans rather than a legally constituted statutory body, with statutory establishment coming via later legislation. That reading contradicts the claim's own wording, which asks for a public announcement of establishment 'as part of its proposed overhaul' — explicitly a proposal, not an enacted statute; B4's reading would make the claim nearly unsatisfiable in a one-week window. B4's evidence is also partly unreliable, citing a Bill introduction date of 30 June 2026, after the resolution deadline and inconsistent with the parliamentary record. B2 further notes the announcement itself described a statutory body with statutory powers to prioritise, matching the claim's functional language. Residual doubt concerns whether 'statutory' was used at announcement and whether some cited URLs are verified.

The claim asks only whether the UN would officially announce delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza *by* March 31, 2025 — a cumulative deadline, not a requirement that deliveries occur during March. Solvers B1–B4 cite concrete, official UN sources (UN News 6 Feb 2025 reporting 10,000+ aid trucks entered Gaza since the ceasefire; OCHA's 17 March 2025 Phase One report documenting ~42,000 trucks; UNISPAL/UN2720 Mechanism monthly overviews showing 13.7K MT delivered in January and 19.5K MT in February 2025). These are unambiguous official UN announcements of actual aid delivery, all predating the deadline. B5's dissent rests on OCHA reports documenting the Israeli blockade from March 2 onward — accurate, but it answers a different question ("was aid being delivered in March?") rather than the criterion as written. Notably, B5's own cited March 18 OCHA report is itself a UN publication that documents the preceding delivery record, and B2 notes a 25-truck convoy delivering 209 MT on 2 March. The blockade evidence does not negate the January–February announcements. Minority position is weaker on the criteria as written.

All five solvers agree on the underlying facts of Little v. Llano County: the June 6, 2024 three-judge Fifth Circuit panel ruled partly against the county (8 of 17 books ordered returned); that panel opinion was vacated on July 3, 2024 when en banc rehearing was granted; en banc oral argument was held September 24, 2024; and the en banc court did not rule (10-7 for the county) until May 23, 2025 — long after the October 3, 2024 deadline. The factual record is thus not in dispute; only the mapping to an answer is. B4 treats the pending status as UNRESOLVABLE, but that conflates 'outcome unknown at the time' with 'question unanswerable.' The claim asks whether the county *will have succeeded* by the stated date; a deadline-bound claim whose triggering event has not occurred by the deadline resolves NO. As of October 2, 2024, no appellate ruling in the county's favor existed and the district court's injunction requiring the books on shelves remained the operative legal status, so the county had not succeeded. B1, B2, B3 and B5 apply this correctly and cite the same well-sourced timeline (Statesman, US News, Texas Tribune, Justia docket entries).

Four of five solvers converge on YES, anchored on the same substantive data point: Kpler-sourced reporting that India's Russian crude imports averaged ~1.63 million bpd month-to-date through September 24, 2025 (vs ~1.71 mbpd in August), a window that necessarily contains September 12-18. Bloomberg's full-month tally (~1.6 mbpd) and Reuters reporting that Indian refiners planned to raise September Russian purchases 10-20% over August both point the same direction, and Kpler's own Sept 24 blog cited ~1.8 mbpd flows to India since July. No solver produced pre- or post-cutoff evidence of a mid-September slump; the only downside data point (a ~1.44 mbpd full-month Kpler figure cited by B2 and B5) conflicts with the better-attested ~1.6 mbpd monthly figure and, even if accurate, would reflect the late-September decline after Ukrainian drone strikes reported around Sept 24 — after the target week. B5's abstention rests on a strict pre-cutoff-publication admissibility rule that is not part of the claim's stated criteria; the claim asks what the shipping data show for that week, and the data available at resolution comfortably clear 1.5 mbpd. The main residual risk is that no solver produced an isolated weekly Kpler/Vortexa figure for Sept 12-18, and weekly arrival data is lumpy — a single week can swing well below a monthly mean. That caps confidence rather than reversing the direction.

The claim asks whether the US reported >20,000 new COVID-19 cases on March 30, 2020. Four of five solvers reconstruct the daily increase from consecutive cumulative snapshots and converge on roughly 21,000–23,000 new cases (e.g., CNN tally 137,047 → 160,008; JHU-based series ~140,900 → ~161,800), all above the 20,000 threshold. This matches the well-documented JHU trajectory (Mar 29 ~140.9k, Mar 30 ~161.8k, Mar 31 ~188.2k, Apr 1 213,372, with the widely cited +25,200 day on Mar 31), which brackets March 30's increase at ~21,000. The dissenting solver B4 arrived at 18,099 by differencing two morning-snapshot press briefings with inconsistent as-of times (125,433 for Mar 29 is a stale/lagged figure inconsistent with every other tracker, including the ~137k–141k end-of-March-29 counts cited by the other solvers), so its baseline is misaligned rather than authoritative. The margin over the threshold is modest (~1,000–3,000 cases) and snapshot-timing differences across trackers introduce some risk, which caps confidence, but the weight of same-source day-over-day comparisons supports YES.

Four of five solvers converge on NO, and their evidence is more directly responsive to the claim's wording than B1's YES. The shared primary source (NWS Northern Indiana, weather.gov/iwx/April2026Flooding) gives a rounded areal range of "3 to 6 inches" for March 31–April 4 — and, per B2, the highest binned category on the accompanying rainfall map is "5 to 6 inches," meaning no mapped area was placed above 6 inches. Every specific point measurement surfaced by any solver falls short: localized maxima "exceeding 5.5 inches" (140 mm) in Steuben/Noble/Kosciusko/Whitley counties IN (Watchers, published April 6, i.e., inside the window), 3–5 inches across NW Ohio per NWS Cleveland, ~4.5–5.2 inches at Napoleon OH, ~1.9 inches at Fort Wayne, up to 4 inches in Steuben County NY. B1's two supporting props do not survive scrutiny: (1) the top of a rounded areal range is not a confirmation that any location reached 6.00 inches, and is contradicted by the map's 5–6 inch top bin; (2) the Ohio State Climate Office "6–10 inches" figure is an April monthly accumulation, not attributable to the March 31–April 3 system — B4 independently shows the same aggregation trap for Chicago's 6.46-inch April total (2.43 inches of which fell on April 14). Residual uncertainty is real: the threshold was missed by only ~0.5 inch, the window used by the official summary (through April 4) is looser than the claim's, and an unsurfaced CoCoRaHS or LSR point report crossing 6.00 inches is plausible for an event of this scale. That keeps confidence moderate rather than high, but the claim requires affirmative public confirmation by April 6, and no solver produced one.

All five solvers agree on the underlying facts: on Sept 25–27, 2024, Reuters (corroborated by Japan Times, CNBC, The Defense Post, Ukrainska Pravda, Foreign Policy) published an exclusive based on European intelligence sources and leaked documents revealing that IEMZ Kupol/Almaz-Antey was secretly developing and producing the Garpiya-3 attack drone in China, with plans for a Kashgar facility; the White House responded publicly the same day. The disagreement is purely interpretive, not evidentiary. B4/B5 read "Russia reveal" as requiring an official Russian disclosure — which never happened (Russia stayed silent, China denied knowledge). B1/B2/B3 read it as the standard headline-derived formulation ("Russia's secret war drones project in China revealed"), satisfied a week before the Oct 3 cutoff. With no published resolution criteria, the question is almost certainly auto-generated from the Reuters headline "Russia has secret war drones project in China, intel sources say," and such questions resolve on whether the reported revelation occurred by the deadline — it did. The strict-agency reading rests on a wording artifact rather than any stated criterion. Adopting the YES position, which also comes from the three stronger-model solvers using independent strategies (default, adversarial, criteria), but with confidence tempered by the genuine ambiguity in the verb "reveal."

Solver B2 supplies the only specific, verifiable outcome evidence: the GnosisDAO forum's own GIP-3 thread was created because "the first GIP was not accepted as the required 10% of YES GNO was not reached," and The Defiant independently reported that the 5% airdrop proposal failed to reach the requisite votes since only Gnosis employees voted. A governance-internal admission of failure plus independent reporting outweighs B1/B3's purely inferential case (thread status "Closed", voter self-interest, and an assumed later merkledrop execution — which conflates GIP-1 with subsequent Gnosis distributions). B5's own cited evidence (futarchy market predicting -31.61% impact) further corroborates a negative outcome. B4/B5 abstained only from failure to retrieve tallies, not from any contradicting evidence. Timing fits: voting ran through ~Nov 30, 2020, before the Dec 2 cutoff, and quorum-lowering follow-up proposals appeared immediately after.

The claim requires a UKHSA public announcement, on or before 23 March 2026, that WGS confirmed the Canterbury MenB strain is genetically distinct. Three solvers (B1, B2, B5) independently converge on a coherent timeline: outbreak genome released to public repositories 20 March, hybrid assembly 22 March, and UKHSA's formal WGS-based distinctness statement appearing in Technical Briefing 1 published 24 March (data cutoff 23 March), with SMC expert reaction 24 March and The Conversation explainer 25 March. B2 adds a distinct source class showing that on the deadline date itself (Euronews, 23 March) authorities were still hedged: the strain 'may have significant genetic differences but further analysis is required.' On the YES side, B3 is weak — it attributes 'clearly distinct within this subtype, having multiple potentially significant genetic differences' to the 18 March UKHSA blog, but that exact phrasing is reported by B5 as appearing in Technical Briefing 1 (24 March), and B1/B5 both read the 18 March blog as saying genomic studies were still forthcoming; a WGS distinctness conclusion on 18 March also predates genome release. B4 is the strongest YES evidence — a dated primary source (parliament.uk written statement hcws1434, 23 March, ~80 genetic differences) — but it is a written ministerial statement to Parliament, not an announcement by UKHSA, which the claim names as the announcing body. Weighing the corroborated timeline plus the hedged 23 March UKHSA-sourced press language against a single ministerial-statement citation, the claim as literally worded fails by roughly one day. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the margin is one day and because a lenient resolver treating the ministerial statement as a government/UKHSA announcement could plausibly score this YES.

All five solvers agree on the underlying facts: the only Manchester City vs Slovan Bratislava fixture in this window was the UEFA Champions League league-phase match played 1 October 2024, which Manchester City won 4-0 (Gündogan, Foden, Haaland, McAtee). This is corroborated by ESPN, Man City's official match report, Fox Sports, Soccerway, Goal, Transfermarkt and Sports Mole — all published before the 2024-10-11 deadline. No match between these clubs occurred on 9 October 2024.

The only dispute is interpretive. B5 answers UNRESOLVABLE on the grounds that "dates are binding" and the question must resolve exactly as worded. But the prompt explicitly states no resolution criteria were published beyond the question itself, so B5 is applying a criterion it invented rather than one it was given.
